newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain may undershoot government deficit goal.
newsitem.headline: Spain may undershoot government deficit goal.

text.p: Despite initial deviations, Spain's central government budget deficit is now so well on track it could even undershoot the initial ceiling, helping the country meet the overall single currency deficit target.

For 1997, Spain budgeted the central government deficit at 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, with social security and the regional deficit at 0.5 percent, bringing the total to the threshold of the single currency requirement of 3.0 percent.
The two peripheral deficits now risk an overshoot, but the central state may offer the solution.

"The (last) data look ok, especially on the revenue side....It's even possible the government could engine an undershooting of the central government budget deficit target in a way to compensate for the social security deficit," said Colin Warren at Tokai Bank in London.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Spanish Economy Minister announced an accumulated budget on a cash basis through May at 967 billion pesetas, 10.9 percent narrower than in the same year-ago period.
On a national account basis, Spain had a similar figure standing at 967.1 billion pesetas, which corresponds to 1.2 percent of the estimated 1997 gross domestic product.

"Revenues are higher than what was initially budgeted, while expenditures are in line with the budget. So the conclusion is that the central budget deficit will meet its target," said Jose Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers.

In accumulated terms, revenues were up 14.4 percent, with direct taxes up 14.4 percent and indirect tax up 7.6 percent. That compares with 7.1 percent and 8.3 percent, respectively, forecast in the budget.

Value-added-tax receipts, which climbed 8.6 percent in the first five months of 1997, were seen as solid proof the economy was picking up and that official forecasts for an eight-percent rise in the year would be met.
On the expenditure side, analysts said seasonal factors were speeding up the trend, but they were expecting it to slow soon.
"Primary surplus improvement is really impressive," said Tokai's Warren.
The primary surplus rose in the first five month to 668.9 billion pesetas, or 117.2 percent over the 1996 same period.
Earlier in June, Budget Secretary Jose Folgado said Spain's budget deficit on a cash basis would narrow sharply from July and that by the year-end it would be down 40 percent.

But by meeting the central government budget target, Spain will only be half-way to meeting the convergence criteria. The most difficult target now seems to be the meeting of social security and regional government goals.
"..the situation of the local authorities and social security is less clear...analysis is complicated by the absence of firm, timely data," a recent Lehman Brother's note said.

Recent local press reports showed Spain's social security had an extra deficit of 35 billion pesetas in the first quarter of 1997 due to higher-than-expected payouts for temporary incapacity of workers.
In 1996, the social security deficit was 0.5 percent of GDP, or 350 billion pesetas, and well above the 0.3 percent initially forecast. For this year the target stands at 0.2 percent of GDP.
"As happened in the past year, the higher risk stands in the social security deficit," Alzola said.
"Although the risk is now lower than one year ago because the sharp rise in new jobs is expected to boost social security payments" he added.
